南亞／印度（奧里薩、西孟加拉、阿薩姆、曼尼普爾）: South Asia / India (Odisha, West Bengal, Assam, Manipur)
演奏時以雙手手掌與手指擊奏，右面發高音，左面發低音。初學先分別控制兩面擊點與力度: It is played with the palms and fingers of both hands, the right head giving the high note and the left the low. A beginner first controls the striking point and the force on each head separately, so that the high note is clear and the low steady. If the larger head sounds too high, the edge of the head can be wetted with the fingers and left for a few minutes, or stretched with the palm, so that it slackens and gives a lower note.

科爾鼓主要用於北印度與東印度虔敬音樂伴奏。在阿薩姆，它是一神信仰文化的重要樂器，: The khol is used mainly to accompany devotional music in North and East India. In Assam it is an important instrument of the one-god faith, appearing in bhaona drama, in gayan and prasanga recitation, in narrative kirtan and in the borgeet lyric songs, and it also accompanies Sattriya dance; Sankardev changed the wooden drum to earthenware and used it with cymbals in gayan and prasanga recitation. In Odisha it is common in the arati rites of Vishnu, Jagannath and Radha-Krishna temples, and it accompanies Odia and Bengali kirtan and Gaudi dance. In ISKCON and Gaudiya Vaishnava circles it is the main drum for bhajan and kirtan.
科爾鼓兩面音高不同：右面音高較高，帶金屬感；左面較大，音高較低，呈低音。鼓面以牛: The two heads of the khol are at different pitches: the right head is higher and has a metallic quality, the left is larger, lower and serves as the bass. The heads are of cowhide or goatskin and are coated with a mixture of rice paste, glue and iron. Tuning depends on moisture: when damp the large head slackens, vibrates more and sounds lower; when dry it tightens and sounds higher. The player can adjust it by wetting the rim or stretching it with the palm. It is played with the palms and fingers of both hands; the source does not say how volume is controlled.

The khol is a double-headed earthenware membranophone of Odisha, West Bengal, Assam and Manipur in South Asia, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.23. Its body is hollow with cowhide or goatskin on both ends, one large and one small, and it is played with the palms and fingers of both hands; the right head has a metallic pitch, the left a thicker bass. It is used to accompany devotional music, appearing in Assam in bhaona drama, gayan-bayan, prasanga-kirtan and the borgeets, and it also accompanies Sattriya performance; in the Vishnu temples of Odisha the arati rites, kirtan and bhajan are also commonly accompanied by it.
科爾鼓為兩面鼓，傳統琴身以陶土製成，中空，兩端蒙皮，其中一面明顯較小。鼓面多用牛: The khol is a two-headed drum; its traditional body is of earthenware, hollow, with skin on both ends, one of them clearly smaller. The heads are usually cowhide or goatskin, of three layers, treated with a circular tuning paste made of rice paste, glue and iron. Some modern instruments use a fibreglass body and synthetic heads; the source does not state the materials of the other parts.
科爾鼓起源於印度東北與東部，見於奧里薩、西孟加拉、阿薩姆與曼尼普爾。起源有多種說: The khol originates in northeastern and eastern India and is found in Odisha, West Bengal, Assam and Manipur. There are several accounts of its origin, and different regions developed different forms. In Assam, Sankardev turned the wooden khol into an earthenware one and brought it into the Ek Saran Naam Dharma faith, where it is used in bhaona drama, the gayan-bayan sung exchanges, prasanga-kirtan narrative recitation and the borgeet lyric songs. It is also used in the arati rites of Vishnu temples in Odisha, in Odia and Bengali kirtan, and in the bhajan and kirtan of ISKCON and the Gaudiya Vaishnavas.
